theory.overview: The processor-memory performance gap has grown exponentially: CPUs improved 1000x faster than DRAM. Cache memory bridges this gap by exploiting locality—storing frequently and recently accessed data in small, fast SRAM close to the processor. When the CPU needs data, it checks cache first. On a hit, data arrives in 1-10 cycles. On a miss, a slow memory access (100+ cycles) is required. With hit rates of 95%+, caches make memory appear nearly as fast as SRAM while maintaining DRAM capacity. Understanding cache design—mapping, replacement, coherence—is essential for high-performance software and hardware.

sections.title: The Locality Principles
sections.content: Caches work because programs exhibit locality. Temporal locality means recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon (loops, counters). Spatial locality means data near recently accessed data is likely to be accessed (arrays, sequential code). Caches exploit temporal locality by keeping recently used data, and spatial locality by fetching blocks (cache lines) containing multiple adjacent words.

sections.title: Cache Organization
sections.content: A cache consists of sets, each containing one or more cache lines (blocks). Each cache line stores data plus metadata: tag (identifies which memory address), valid bit (line contains valid data), and dirty bit (modified, needs writeback). The memory address splits into tag, index (selects set), and offset (selects byte within line). The index bits find the set, then tags are compared in parallel to detect a hit.

sections.title: Mapping Strategies
sections.content: Direct-mapped caches assign each memory block to exactly one cache line (simple but can conflict). Fully associative caches allow any block in any line (flexible but expensive comparators). Set-associative caches compromise: n-way set associative allows each block in any of n lines within a set. Most CPUs use 2-way, 4-way, or 8-way set associative caches.

types.direct: 1-way: each block has exactly one location
types.setAssociative: n-way: block in any of n locations within set

sections.title: Replacement and Write Policies
sections.content: When a new block enters a full set, a replacement policy chooses which existing block to evict. LRU (Least Recently Used) is effective but complex; pseudo-LRU approximates with less overhead. Write policies handle stores: write-through immediately updates both cache and memory (simple, slower); write-back marks cache as dirty and writes to memory only on eviction (faster, needs dirty bit).

write.writeBack: Update cache only, write to memory on eviction

sections.title: Cache Hierarchy: L1, L2, L3
sections.content: Modern CPUs have multiple cache levels. L1 (split into instruction and data caches) is smallest (16-64KB), fastest (2-4 cycles), and closest to the core. L2 is larger (256KB-1MB), slower (10-20 cycles), and unified or per-core. L3 is largest (4-64MB shared), slowest (30-50 cycles), and shared among cores. Each level filters accesses to the next, with L1 hitting ~90%, L2 catching most of the rest, and only ~1% reaching main memory.

sections.title: Cache Miss Types
sections.content: Not all misses are equal. Compulsory (cold start) misses occur on first access to a block—unavoidable but can be reduced by prefetching. Capacity misses occur because the working set exceeds cache size—would be hits in larger cache. Conflict misses occur due to mapping limitations—even with space available, multiple blocks map to the same set. Understanding these guides cache-friendly code optimization.

missTypes.capacity: Cache too small for working set

keyConcepts.name: Hit Rate
keyConcepts.description: Percentage of memory accesses found in cache. Good caches achieve 90-98%.

keyConcepts.name: AMAT
keyConcepts.description: Average Memory Access Time. Combines hit time and miss penalty weighted by hit rate.
keyConcepts.formula: AMAT = Hit Time + (Miss Rate × Miss Penalty)

keyConcepts.name: Cache Line/Block
keyConcepts.description: Unit of cache storage. Typically 32-128 bytes, holding multiple words to exploit spatial locality.

keyConcepts.name: Associativity
keyConcepts.description: Number of cache lines in a set. Higher associativity reduces conflicts but increases complexity.

steps.title: Address Split
steps.description: Divide memory address into tag, index, and offset fields.

steps.title: Index to Set
steps.description: Use index bits to select which cache set to examine.

steps.title: Tag Comparison
steps.description: Compare all tags in the set with the address tag in parallel.

steps.title: Hit or Miss
steps.description: If any tag matches and valid bit is set, it's a hit. Otherwise, it's a miss.

practiceProblems.title: Cache Purpose
practiceProblems.description: What problem does cache memory solve?
practiceProblems.explanation: Cache bridges the performance gap between fast CPUs and slow main memory by storing frequently accessed data in fast SRAM close to the processor.

practiceProblems.title: Temporal Locality
practiceProblems.answer: Recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again
practiceProblems.explanation: Temporal locality means if a memory location is accessed, it's likely to be accessed again soon. Caches exploit this by keeping recently used data.

practiceProblems.title: Direct-Mapped Cache
practiceProblems.description: In a direct-mapped cache, how many locations can a memory block map to?
practiceProblems.explanation: Direct-mapped (1-way set associative) means each memory block maps to exactly one cache line. Simple but prone to conflicts.

practiceProblems.title: AMAT Calculation
practiceProblems.description: If hit time is 2 cycles, miss rate is 5%, and miss penalty is 100 cycles, what is AMAT?
practiceProblems.explanation: AMAT = Hit Time + (Miss Rate × Miss Penalty) = 2 + (0.05 × 100) = 2 + 5 = 7 cycles.
hints: AMAT = Hit Time + (Miss Rate × Miss Penalty)

practiceProblems.title: Cache Line Size
practiceProblems.description: Why are cache lines larger than a single word?
practiceProblems.explanation: Fetching blocks of data exploits spatial locality—if one byte is accessed, nearby bytes are likely to be accessed soon. Reduces compulsory misses.

practiceProblems.title: Write-Back vs Write-Through
practiceProblems.description: Which write policy has lower memory bandwidth requirements?
practiceProblems.explanation: Write-back only writes to memory on eviction, reducing bandwidth. Write-through updates memory on every store, using more bandwidth but ensuring consistency.

minigame.title: Cache Champion
minigame.description: Optimize cache performance! Manage cache lines, handle hits and misses, and maximize hit rate. Choose replacement policies wisely and watch your AMAT improve!
instructions: Memory requests appear from the CPU
Watch the address break down into tag, index, and offset
See which cache set is accessed
Observe hit or miss - aim for high hit rate!
On miss, choose replacement policy (LRU, FIFO, Random)
Track AMAT and optimize cache configuration!

snippets.title: Cache Simulator
snippets.code:
class CacheLine:
    def __init__(self):
        self.valid = False
        self.tag = 0
        self.data = bytearray(64)  # 64-byte line
        self.dirty = False
        self.lru_counter = 0

class Cache:
    def __init__(self, size_kb, associativity, line_size, write_policy='write_back'):
        self.size = size_kb * 1024
        self.associativity = associativity
        self.line_size = line_size
        self.num_sets = self.size // (associativity * line_size)
        self.sets = [[CacheLine() for _ in range(associativity)] 
                     for _ in range(self.num_sets)]
        self.write_policy = write_policy
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0
        self.access_count = 0
    
    def _split_address(self, addr):
        offset_bits = (self.line_size - 1).bit_length()
        index_bits = (self.num_sets - 1).bit_length()
        
        offset = addr & (self.line_size - 1)
        index = (addr >> offset_bits) & (self.num_sets - 1)
        tag = addr >> (offset_bits + index_bits)
        
        return tag, index, offset
    
    def access(self, addr, is_write=False):
        self.access_count += 1
        tag, index, offset = self._split_address(addr)
        
        # Check all ways in set
        cache_set = self.sets[index]
        for way in cache_set:
            if way.valid and way.tag == tag:
                # Cache hit!
                self.hits += 1
                way.lru_counter = self.access_count
                if is_write:
                    way.dirty = True
                    if self.write_policy == 'write_through':
                        pass  # Would write to memory here
                return True
        
        # Cache miss
        self.misses += 1
        self._handle_miss(cache_set, tag, is_write)
        return False
    
    def _handle_miss(self, cache_set, tag, is_write):
        # Find replacement victim (LRU)
        victim_idx = min(range(len(cache_set)), 
                        key=lambda i: cache_set[i].lru_counter if cache_set[i].valid else -1)
        victim = cache_set[victim_idx]
        
        # Write back if dirty
        if victim.valid and victim.dirty:
            pass  # Would write to memory
        
        # Load new line
        victim.valid = True
        victim.tag = tag
        victim.dirty = is_write
        victim.lru_counter = self.access_count
    
    def get_stats(self):
        total = self.hits + self.misses
        hit_rate = self.hits / total if total > 0 else 0
        return {
            'hits': self.hits,
            'misses': self.misses,
            'hit_rate': hit_rate,
            'miss_rate': 1 - hit_rate
        }

# Test with array access pattern
cache = Cache(size_kb=4, associativity=4, line_size=64)

# Sequential access (good spatial locality)
print('Sequential access:')
for i in range(256):
    addr = i * 4  # 4-byte words
    cache.access(addr)
stats = cache.get_stats()
print(f'  Hit rate: {stats["hit_rate"]:.2%}')

# Random access (poor locality)
cache2 = Cache(size_kb=4, associativity=4, line_size=64)
print('Random access:')
import random
for _ in range(256):
    addr = random.randint(0, 1024) * 4
    cache2.access(addr)
stats2 = cache2.get_stats()
print(f'  Hit rate: {stats2["hit_rate"]:.2%}')
